\chapter{Five Things You Can Pick Up}
\label{ch:el-oro-y-la-botella}
\hlchaptermodality{373}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can say el oro, la botella, la alfombra, la falda and el peine, and name five ordinary things I can pick up.}

Complete ES-C373-peine: name five ordinary things you can pick up, and say what each is for.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[el oro]{el oro — named after the colour of dawn}

\label{lesson:ES-C373-oro}



\begin{quote}
Say \emph{pale}, then \emph{smooth}. (\emph{Pálido}; \emph{suave}.)
\end{quote}

\subsection*{What to know first}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item el dinero — what it stands behind.
  \item la moneda — the shape it usually takes.
\end{itemize}

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{O-ro}, two beats with the weight on the first. The \emph{r} between vowels is a single tap, never rolled. $\to$ pronunciation reference
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{el oro} — \textquotedblleft{}gold.\textquotedblright{}

Latin \textbf{aurum}, and behind \emph{aurum} an ancient root meaning \textbf{to shine, to dawn}. Gold was not named for its weight or its rarity or its price. It was named for looking like the first light of the morning.

The same root, barely disguised, is \textbf{aurora} — the dawn, and the aurora borealis, which is dawn where dawn has no business being.

And, far enough back to need reconstructing, English \textbf{east} belongs to it too. The east is the shining place. Gold, the dawn and a compass direction all come from one idea about light.

English took the Latin word by a couple of side doors, both through French:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item an \textbf{oriole} is \emph{aureolus}, \textquotedblleft{}a little golden one,\textquotedblright{} named for the bird's colour;
  \item an \textbf{aureole} is the ring of gold light a painter puts round a head. Same Latin word, different job.
\end{itemize}

The shortest survival is on the periodic table. Gold's symbol is \textbf{Au} — the first two letters of \emph{aurum}, sitting in a chemistry textbook long after Latin stopped being spoken. Chemistry kept the Roman name for a metal the Romans measured their world in.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
You can now name the metal behind the money: \emph{el oro}.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{el oro}
  \item \emph{de oro}
  \item \emph{una moneda de oro}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What did the root behind \emph{aurum} mean? (To shine, to dawn.) And which two letters does gold get on the periodic table? (\emph{Au}, from \emph{aurum}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[la botella]{la botella — and the servant who kept it}

\label{lesson:ES-C373-botella}



\begin{quote}
Say \emph{smooth}, then \emph{gold}. (\emph{Suave}; \emph{el oro}.)
\end{quote}

\subsection*{What to know first}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item el vino — the reason the word exists.
  \item el agua — what is in it now.
\end{itemize}

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{bo-TE-lla}, three beats with the weight on the second. The \emph{ll} is a \emph{y} sound across most of the Spanish-speaking world. $\to$ pronunciation reference
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{la botella} — \textquotedblleft{}the bottle.\textquotedblright{}

Late Latin had \textbf{buttis}, a cask, and a diminutive \textbf{butticula}, a little cask. French turned that into \emph{bouteille}, and Spanish borrowed the French word in the eighteenth century — recently, as these things go.

Spanish already had the same Latin word, inherited by mouth: \textbf{la bota}, the leather wineskin. So \emph{bota} and \emph{botella} are one word twice, the old one worn smooth by centuries of use and the new one arriving with a French accent.

English took the French word too, as \textbf{bottle} — and took something better with it. A \textbf{butler} is \emph{bouteillier}, \textbf{the bottle-man}: the servant in charge of the wine. He had the keys to the cellar, which is a position of trust, and trust promotes; over a few centuries the bottle-keeper rose to running the entire household and kept his old name.

English \textbf{butt}, a large cask, is the same family again, also through French.

One near neighbour that is not a relative. \textbf{El botón}, the button, comes from a Frankish verb meaning to thrust or push — because a button is pushed through. It is a relative of the English verb to \textbf{butt}, as a goat does, and no relation at all to \emph{butt} the cask. Two English \emph{butt}s, two families, and Spanish keeps them apart cleanly.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
You can now ask for a bottle of something: \emph{una botella de agua}.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{la botella}
  \item \emph{una botella}
  \item \emph{una botella de agua}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What is a butler, taken literally? (The bottle-keeper.) And which Spanish word is the inherited form of the same Latin cask? (\emph{La bota}, the wineskin.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[la alfombra]{la alfombra — and a red that was never there}

\label{lesson:ES-C373-alfombra}



\begin{quote}
Say \emph{gold}, then \emph{the bottle}. (\emph{El oro}; \emph{la botella}.)
\end{quote}

\subsection*{What to know first}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item la almohada — its neighbour, which carries the same Arabic article.
  \item el piso — what it lies on.
\end{itemize}

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{al-FOM-bra}, three beats with the weight on the second. The \emph{mb} runs together, and the \emph{r} is a single tap. $\to$ pronunciation reference
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{la alfombra} — \textquotedblleft{}the rug, the carpet.\textquotedblright{}

The \emph{al-} on the front is the Arabic definite article, brought across stuck to the noun — the same passenger that rides in on \emph{almohada} and on \emph{azúcar}. Spanish then puts its own article in front of it, so \emph{la alfombra} has two.

The noun underneath is Andalusi Arabic \textbf{alḥánbal}, a kind of hanging or tapestry laid over a dais.

Now the part that makes this word worth a lesson. For a long time the dictionaries printed a different story: that \emph{alfombra} came from an Arabic phrase meaning \textbf{the red one}. It is a lovely story. A carpet named for its colour, a red carpet before there were red carpets.

Corominas took it apart, and the way he did it is the lesson. The redness, he pointed out, had been read \textbf{out of} the proposed etymology and then offered back as evidence \textbf{for} it. Nobody had found a red carpet and then looked for a word; somebody had found a word that could mean red and then imagined the carpet. The Academy's dictionary now prints the tapestry word instead.

What produced the mistake was a real word standing nearby. Spanish also had \textbf{alhamar}, a coverlet, and \emph{that} one genuinely does come from the Arabic root for \textbf{red}. The two got tangled in the record, and the redness walked from one word to the other.

Keep both halves: the rug, and the reminder that a beautiful etymology is the kind most worth checking.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
You can now name what is on the floor: \emph{la alfombra}.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{la alfombra}
  \item \emph{una alfombra}
  \item \emph{la alfombra está en el piso}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What is the \emph{al-} of \emph{alfombra}? (The Arabic article, carried in with the noun.) And which nearby word really is the one meaning red? (\emph{Alhamar}, a coverlet.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[la falda]{la falda — the folded thing}

\label{lesson:ES-C373-falda}



\begin{quote}
Say \emph{the bottle}, then \emph{the rug}. (\emph{La botella}; \emph{la alfombra}.)
\end{quote}

\subsection*{What to know first}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item la ropa — the class it belongs to.
  \item el vestido — its nearest neighbour in a wardrobe.
\end{itemize}

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{FAL-da}, two beats with the weight on the first. The \emph{l} is light and forward, and the \emph{d} after it is soft. $\to$ pronunciation reference
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{la falda} — \textquotedblleft{}the skirt.\textquotedblright{}

This is a \textbf{Germanic} word, not a Latin one. It came into Spanish from one of the Germanic languages that arrived in the peninsula — which one is not settled, with Frankish and Gothic both proposed — and it meant a \textbf{fold}.

A skirt is the folded thing: cloth hung in pleats. Spanish still uses \emph{falda} for the lower slope of a mountain, where the ground falls away in folds, which is the older picture showing through.

English \textbf{fold} is the inherited cousin of that same Germanic word — never borrowed, come straight down the English line. So \emph{falda} and \emph{fold} are one word travelling by two routes: one carried into Spain by settlers, the other carried into England the ordinary way.

And here is the look-alike to refuse. \textbf{Falso}, false, begins with the same three letters and has nothing to do with it. \emph{Falso} is Latin \emph{falsus}, from \emph{fallere}, to deceive — the word behind English \textbf{fault}, \textbf{fail} and \textbf{fallacy}.

The two \emph{f}'s are not even the same kind of \emph{f}. One grew out of a Germanic sound and one out of a Latin one, arriving at the same letter from opposite directions. Three shared letters, two families, no relationship.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
You can now name another piece of clothing: \emph{la falda}.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{la falda}
  \item \emph{una falda}
  \item \emph{la falda es gris}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What did \emph{falda} mean before it meant a skirt? (A fold.) And is \emph{falso} a relative? (No — it comes from Latin \emph{fallere}, to deceive.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[el peine]{el peine — the comb, and a story about money}

\label{lesson:ES-C373-peine}



\begin{quote}
Say \emph{the rug}, then \emph{the skirt}. (\emph{La alfombra}; \emph{la falda}.)
\end{quote}

\subsection*{What to know first}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item la cabeza — what it is for.
  \item la mano — what holds it.
\end{itemize}

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{PEI-ne}, two beats with the weight on the first. The \emph{ei} is one glide, close to the vowel of English \emph{hay}. $\to$ pronunciation reference
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{el peine} — \textquotedblleft{}the comb.\textquotedblright{}

Latin \textbf{pecten}, a comb, from \textbf{pectere}, to comb — used of hair and of wool, since carding wool is combing it. English keeps the word in \textbf{pectinate}, a botanist's and anatomist's term for anything shaped like a comb.

So far so ordinary. Now a story, offered as a story.

Latin also had \textbf{pecū}, livestock, and a long tradition joins it to this comb-word, on the reasoning that a sheep is the animal you \textbf{pluck}. If that holds, then \emph{peine} is a distant relative of a whole family about money:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{pecuniary}, to do with money, from \emph{pecūnia} — because a Roman's wealth was counted in animals before it was counted in coins;
  \item \textbf{peculiar}, from \emph{pecūlium}, the private property a son or a slave was allowed to keep. Something peculiar is something \textbf{your own}, and the sense of odd came from there by way of distinctive;
  \item \textbf{peculate}, to embezzle — helping yourself to the herd.
\end{itemize}

English has the same idea by its own road: \textbf{fee} was Old English \emph{feoh}, which meant cattle, then property, then money.

The caution belongs with the story. Specialists no longer agree that the combing half and the livestock half were ever one word; some now treat the wealth sense as the original and the animals as second. So take the money family as a \textbf{tradition} rather than a fact — which is worth knowing in itself, because a great many etymologies people repeat with confidence are exactly this: an old, tidy, widely printed proposal that the current specialists have quietly stopped endorsing.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
You can now name the thing on the shelf: \emph{el peine}.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{el peine}
  \item \emph{un peine}
  \item \emph{el peine está en la mano}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What did Latin \emph{pecū} mean? (Livestock.) And is the link between the comb and the money words a fact? (No — a long tradition that specialists no longer agree on.)
\end{tcolorbox}
